SCALING_MODEL: O(1) per request append; list grows with request count, bounded by max_turns in practice.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has no usage accounting in its event model; this is a green-field pattern.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: CRX's journal records what happened; the SDK shows cost belongs beside the model-call record, per request, with retry visibility. No conflict, pure addition.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: add per-request usage entries to CRX model-call events.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Low-medium: enables cost attribution CRX currently cannot do.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Make three model calls with one retry and assert four RequestUsage entries whose token sums equal the run totals.

PROBLEM: An unbounded agent loop must terminate deterministically and leave evidence of why it stopped.
MECHANISM: max_turns is checked per turn; exceeding it attaches a SpanError (Max turns exceeded, with the limit) to the current agent span and raises MaxTurnsExceeded. Configured RunErrorHandlers can instead synthesize a final output, which is validated against the agent's output schema before being committed. The streamed path records whether the handler ran. Source: https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/32edd3c3ecde37a7fb6bf4b082f35f1d8f7f086b/src/agents/run_internal/run_loop.py; https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/32edd3c3ecde37a7fb6bf4b082f35f1d8f7f086b/src/agents/exceptions.py; https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/32edd3c3ecde37a7fb6bf4b082f35f1d8f7f086b/src/agents/run_error_handlers.py
INVARIANT: A run that exceeds max_turns always terminates and always leaves either the exception or a validated synthesized output plus the span error; it never loops silently.
FAILURE_MODEL: Handler exceptions propagate; a handler that returns invalid output fails validation rather than committing bad output.
SECURITY_MODEL: A synthesized final output is model-visible content produced by policy, not the agent; consumers must be able to distinguish it (it is committed as a message output item like any final output, so downstream readers should check the span error).
SCALING_MODEL: O(1) check per turn.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX already practices bounded automation with typed failure semantics; this corroborates rather than invents.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: No semantic conflict. The SDK's addition is attaching the bound violation to the trace (SpanError on the agent span) so the stop is visible in telemetry, not just in the exception.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: attach bound-violation evidence to CRX's existing typed failures.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Low: small telemetry improvement on a practice CRX already follows.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Set max_turns=1 on a two-turn task and assert MaxTurnsExceeded plus a SpanError on the agent span carrying the limit; configure a handler and assert its output passes schema validation before commit.

PROBLEM: Traces must be useful for debugging without becoming a secret-exfiltration channel when exported to third-party backends.
MECHANISM: trace_include_sensitive_data (default from OPENAI_AGENTS_TRACE_INCLUDE_SENSITIVE_DATA, default true) gates all sensitive payloads: tool call arguments and outputs in function spans, generation inputs/outputs, error message contents (via get_trace_tool_error). Span skeletons (names, types, parent links, triggered flags) are always recorded. Model config URLs are sanitized (auth material and query params stripped) before entering spans. Source: https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/32edd3c3ecde37a7fb6bf4b082f35f1d8f7f086b/src/agents/run_config.py; https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/32edd3c3ecde37a7fb6bf4b082f35f1d8f7f086b/src/agents/run_internal/tool_execution.py; https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/32edd3c3ecde37a7fb6bf4b082f35f1d8f7f086b/src/agents/models/_trace.py
INVARIANT: Disabling the flag removes all sensitive payloads while preserving span structure; no code path can leak arguments into a span when the flag is false.
FAILURE_MODEL: The default is true, so a deployment that never sets the flag exports sensitive data to the configured trace backend by default. Failing closed would be the safer default; the SDK chose debuggability.
SECURITY_MODEL: This is the primary exfiltration control for the trace pipeline; exporters must additionally treat user metadata dicts as untrusted.
SCALING_MODEL: One boolean check per span write; sanitization is O(URL length).
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has fail-closed canonicalization at ingress; the SDK's trace gating is a parallel fail-open-by-default control CRX should invert.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: CRX should adopt the skeleton-always/payload-gated split but default the gate to closed. The SDK's mistake to avoid copying is the default-true.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: split CRX observability payloads into skeleton vs sensitive with a default-closed gate.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: prevents the trace pipeline from becoming a secret leak; the default matters more than the mechanism.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Set trace_include_sensitive_data=false, run a tool-calling agent, and assert function spans exist with names but null input/output; assert a base URL with credentials appears sanitized in generation span config.

PROBLEM: Workflow execution state must survive process, machine, and cluster death without losing exactly-where-we-were.
MECHANISM: Every workflow execution is an append-only event history persisted in the history service. Mutable state is a cache rebuilt on demand by replaying events: MutableStateRebuilder.ApplyEvents(ctx, namespaceID, requestID, execution, history, newRunHistory, newRunID) folds [][]*historypb.HistoryEvent into a fresh MutableState. Nothing about workflow progress lives only in memory.
INVARIANT: History is the source of truth; mutable state is a derived, rebuildable projection. Any replica holding the event log can reconstruct identical state.
FAILURE_MODEL: History service down = no progress but no corruption; on recovery, rebuild from persisted log. Event write is transactional with state update (single shard transaction). Lost in-memory state is a non-event.
SECURITY_MODEL: Namespace-scoped; history is internal. No per-event auth model beyond namespace isolation.
SCALING_MODEL: Sharded by workflow ID hash across history shards; each shard owns its key range. Linear horizontal scale of the history tier.
CRX_ANALOG: Direct analog of CRX ping_events canonical journal. CRX already owns this pattern but lacks per-attempt Run identity and causation_id on mission events. The rebuilder pattern maps to CRX ReplayAuthority: given ping_events for a run, rebuild run state deterministically.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Temporal events are workflow-domain typed (WorkflowTaskScheduled, ActivityTaskStarted...). CRX events are agent-domain typed (mission events). The rebuilder fold is generic; the event vocabulary is CRX-constitutional.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: formalize a RunStateRebuilder that folds ping_events into run state, reusing CRX's existing journal.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: closes the replay gap; makes 'resume a dead run' a fold over existing evidence instead of new machinery.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill a history shard mid-execution in a test cluster; assert a different shard rebuilds identical mutable state from the log and the workflow continues with no duplicate side effects.

PROBLEM: Transient failures should retry with bounded backoff; permanent failures (canceled, terminated, non-retryable types) must never retry.
MECHANISM: common/retrypolicy/retry_policy.go: IsRetryableFailure classifies failures by type. Canceled/terminated never retryable. Timeout failures: only START_TO_CLOSE and HEARTBEAT are retryable (schedule-to-start/schedule-to-close timeouts are not, they indicate capacity problems). Application failures honor a non-retryable flag and a nonRetryableTypes list. EnsureDefaults fills unset fields (initial interval, backoff coefficient 2.0, max interval, max attempts).
INVARIANT: Retryability is a pure function of (failure type, policy). The same failure under the same policy always retries or never retries, regardless of which worker evaluates it.
FAILURE_MODEL: Misclassified non-retryable failure = infinite retry loop bounded only by MaximumAttempts (default 0 = unlimited for activities). This is why MaximumAttempts and nonRetryableTypes are load-bearing.
SECURITY_MODEL: Policy set by workflow author; no privilege boundary.
SCALING_MODEL: Evaluated locally on history service; no coordination needed.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has bounded automation with typed failure semantics but no formal retry classifier. Map: subagent attempt failures get classified (transient vs permanent) by a pure function before any retry; permanent classes (auth failure, policy violation) never retry.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Temporal retries activities/workflows. CRX retries agent attempts and tool calls. The classification table (what is transient) is CRX-constitutional because only CRX knows its failure taxonomy.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: port IsRetryableFailure as a pure function over CRX's typed failure taxonomy; store retry state on the per-attempt Run record.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: eliminates retry storms on permanent failures; makes retry behavior auditable and deterministic.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Feed a CANCELED failure and a HEARTBEAT-timeout failure through the classifier 1000x; assert deterministic identical classification and that CANCELED never schedules a retry timer.

PROBLEM: Detect a dead worker running a long activity without waiting for the full start-to-close timeout.
MECHANISM: Activities declare a HeartbeatTimeout. Workers must heartbeat periodically; the server tracks LastHeartbeatUpdateTime/LastHeartbeatDetails on the activity info. If no heartbeat arrives within the timeout, the history service fires an ActivityTimeoutTask (CategoryTimer, keyed by VisibilityTimestamp) which marks the attempt timed out and schedules a retry. Heartbeat details are delivered to the next attempt so it can resume from progress. ResetHeartbeats flag lets an operator reset heartbeat state when resetting an activity.
INVARIANT: Liveness is proven by periodic heartbeat, not by task completion. Silence past the deadline is indistinguishable from death and is treated as death.
FAILURE_MODEL: Heartbeat timeout too short = false death detection and duplicate execution (at-least-once). Too long = slow detection. Network partition between worker and server looks identical to worker death; heartbeats are the only signal.
SECURITY_MODEL: Heartbeats are authenticated worker-to-server; heartbeat details are opaque blobs (can carry progress checkpoints).
SCALING_MODEL: Timer tasks are sharded with the workflow; visibility timestamp orders the timer queue.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX subagents are activities: long-lived, opaque, killable. CRX currently has no heartbeat/lease on subagent attempts. A subagent heartbeat (progress ping with a details blob) with a server-side timeout gives CRX worker-death detection without polling the child.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Temporal heartbeats carry activity progress. CRX heartbeats should carry the subagent's typed progress summary so the retry attempt can resume with context, not just restart.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: heartbeat endpoint on the run record, timer-queue check for overdue heartbeats, details blob stored on the attempt record.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: closes the largest liveness gap in CRX autonomous execution (dead subagent detected in seconds/minutes, not never).
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Start a subagent attempt with a 30s heartbeat timeout, kill the worker process at 10s, assert the server marks the attempt timed-out and reschedules within ~35s, and that heartbeat details from before death are visible on the retry.

PROBLEM: A workflow worker can die while holding a workflow task (the decision unit). The workflow must not stall forever.
MECHANISM: Every scheduled workflow task carries a WorkflowTaskTimeout (start-to-close). service/history/workflow/workflow_task_state_machine.go: ApplyWorkflowTaskTimedOutEvent records a WorkflowTaskTimedOut history event and the task is rescheduled to the queue. The timeout is recorded IN the history, so replay observes the same timeout the live execution did.
INVARIANT: A workflow task is a lease with a deadline recorded in history. Expiry is itself a history event, so recovery and replay agree on what happened.
FAILURE_MODEL: Timeout too aggressive = duplicate workflow-task execution (safe: tasks are deterministic replays, side effects go through activities). Sticky queues can delay detection if the worker is partitioned but not dead.
SECURITY_MODEL: Internal to history service.
SCALING_MODEL: Timer tasks sharded with workflow.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX's parent-agent decision step is the workflow task. If the parent agent process dies mid-decision, the run stalls. A decision-step lease with timeout + reschedule closes this.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Temporal workflow tasks are deterministic replays, so duplicates are harmless. CRX parent decisions may have side effects; CRX must make the decision step idempotent (record decision intent before acting) before adopting timeout-reschedule.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: decision-step lease on the run record; timeout fires a RunDecisionTimedOut event; reschedule.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: covers parent-death, rarer than subagent death but currently a silent stall.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill the parent agent mid-decision; assert a WorkflowTaskTimedOut-equivalent event appears and a new decision step is scheduled, with no duplicate side effects.

PROBLEM: External actors (humans, other systems) must inject information into a running workflow without polling.
MECHANISM: historyEngineImpl.SignalWorkflowExecution (service/history/history_engine.go:686) appends a WorkflowExecutionSignaled event to the target workflow's history. Signals are durably recorded before delivery; if the workflow is not currently processing, the signal waits in history. Signal handlers are workflow code, so signal processing is replay-deterministic.
INVARIANT: Every signal is a history event. A signal is never 'delivered and lost': it is recorded, then processed, in order.
FAILURE_MODEL: Signal to a closed workflow is rejected. Signal ordering is per-workflow FIFO. Duplicate signal delivery is possible at the transport layer; handler idempotency is the author's job (signal ID dedup is not engine-provided).
SECURITY_MODEL: Namespace-scoped; any holder of namespace credentials can signal any workflow in it. No per-signal authorization.
SCALING_MODEL: Routed to the owning history shard.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX needs exactly this for human approval and external events: an append-only Signal event on the run (causation-linked), processed at the next decision boundary. CRX must add what Temporal lacks: per-signal authorization (action-level auth is a proven CRX gap).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Temporal signals are untyped payloads to workflow code. CRX signals must be typed (approval granted/denied, external event) with an authorization check at ingress and a causation link to the run.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: signal event type in ping_events with causation_id, ingress auth check, delivery at decision boundary.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: the primitive under human approval, external webhooks, and cross-mission messaging.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Signal a run that has no active worker; kill everything; restart; assert the signal is still recorded and processed exactly once at the next decision boundary.

PROBLEM: Long-running workflows accumulate unbounded history; replay cost grows forever.
MECHANISM: MutableStateImpl.AddContinueAsNewEvent (service/history/workflow/mutable_state_impl.go:6309) closes the current run with a WorkflowExecutionContinuedAsNew event that starts a new run with the same workflow ID (new run ID), carrying forward selected state. History stays bounded; the chain of runs is linked.
INVARIANT: Continuation is an explicit event linking old run to new run. The full lineage is traversable; no state is silently dropped (what carries forward is explicit in the event).
FAILURE_MODEL: State not carried forward is lost. Chain traversal is O(depth).
SECURITY_MODEL: Same as workflow start.
SCALING_MODEL: New run may land on a different shard.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX missions can run for days. Continue-as-new maps to run rotation: close run N with a ContinuedAsNew event pointing at run N+1, carrying the compacted mission state. Prevents unbounded context/event growth per run.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Temporal carries workflow arguments forward. CRX must carry the mission's evidence pointers and compacted state, and the linkage must preserve causation lineage (a proven CRX gap).
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-Medium: a run-rotation procedure plus a ContinuedAsNew event type with explicit carried-state schema.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: bounds per-run history; enables multi-day missions without replay degradation.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Run a mission past the rotation threshold; assert run N closes with ContinuedAsNew, run N+1 starts with exactly the declared carried state, and lineage traversal returns the full chain.

PROBLEM: Retried or duplicated start requests must not create duplicate workflow executions.
MECHANISM: StartWorkflowExecution honors WorkflowIdReusePolicy (allow-duplicate, allow-duplicate-failed-only, reject-duplicate) and request-ID dedup: the same request ID returns the existing execution instead of starting a new one. The dedup decision is made transactionally at history write time.
INVARIANT: (workflow ID, request ID) -> at most one execution outcome. Duplicate starts are resolved to the existing execution, not rejected blindly.
FAILURE_MODEL: Request ID collision across different intended workflows returns the wrong execution. Clock skew does not matter (IDs are opaque).
SECURITY_MODEL: Request IDs are client-supplied; no verification.
SCALING_MODEL: Checked on the owning shard.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX MissionRuntime already has idempotent deterministic mission IDs. Extend: per-attempt Run IDs must be deterministic functions of (mission ID, attempt sequence, request ID) so a retried spawn resolves to the existing attempt instead of duplicating.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Temporal dedups workflow starts. CRX must dedup attempt starts AND tool calls (the MCP/tool-execution path gap).
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: deterministic attempt-ID derivation; request-ID column on the attempt record with unique constraint.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: eliminates duplicate subagent spawns on parent retry, the most expensive duplication in CRX.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Issue the same spawn request twice concurrently; assert exactly one attempt record exists and both callers receive the same attempt ID.

PROBLEM: Claim check: does Temporal provide engine-level saga/compensation?
MECHANISM: FALSIFIED. A repo-wide search for saga/compensation in temporalio/temporal server source returns no engine mechanism. Compensation in the Temporal ecosystem is a user-space pattern (saga pattern in workflow code, e.g. in samples), not a server primitive. Any claim that Temporal 'has built-in sagas' is false at the engine level.
INVARIANT: N/A (falsified claim).
FAILURE_MODEL: N/A.
SECURITY_MODEL: N/A.
SCALING_MODEL: N/A.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX should not expect to harvest a compensation engine from Temporal. If CRX needs compensation, the compensation RECORD (what was undone, evidence-linked) is CRX-constitutional; the execution of compensating actions reuses the normal attempt machinery.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: N/A.
INTEGRATION_COST: None.
EXPECTED_VALUE: None as a mechanism; value is in not chasing a phantom.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: grep -ri saga temporalio/temporal/service temporalio/temporal/common -> zero engine hits; only docs/samples references.

PROBLEM: Service code must survive crashes without re-executing completed side effects, without the developer writing explicit checkpointing.
MECHANISM: Every durable operation is a journal entry. crates/types/src/journal/entries.rs defines EntryType: Input, Output, GetState, SetState, ClearState, GetPromise, PeekPromise, CompletePromise, Sleep, Call, OneWayCall, Awakeable, CompleteAwakeable, Run, CancelInvocation, GetCallInvocationId, AttachInvocation, GetInvocationOutput, Custom. On re-invocation after a crash, entries replay from the journal: completed entries return recorded results instead of re-executing. Sleep is a first-class journal entry (durable timer), Awakeable is a journal entry completable from outside.
INVARIANT: Re-execution after failure replays the journal prefix; no completed entry is ever re-executed. The journal is the execution.
FAILURE_MODEL: Journal write must precede the side effect being considered done; otherwise a crash between side effect and journaling causes re-execution (at-least-once for non-recorded effects). Journal corruption = unrecoverable invocation.
SECURITY_MODEL: Journal is internal; entries carry no auth metadata.
SCALING_MODEL: Partitioned by service key; journal stored in the partition store (RocksDB-backed).
CRX_ANALOG: Maps to CRX's missing per-attempt step journal. CRX has mission-level events but no durable per-attempt record of which tool calls/steps completed. A step journal (entry per tool call with recorded output) gives CRX exactly-once step semantics on attempt retry.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Restate journals service-handler operations. CRX must journal agent-attempt operations (tool calls, subagent spawns, file writes) with the attempt ID as the journal key and causation links to mission events.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: step-journal table keyed by attempt ID + step index; replay-on-retry logic in the attempt executor. Cannot copy code (BSL-1.1); reimplement the pattern.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: the core mechanism for UNKNOWN_OUTCOME. A retried attempt replays completed steps instead of redoing (and double-paying for) tool calls.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill an attempt mid-way through 3 tool calls (2 recorded, 1 in-flight); retry; assert the 2 recorded calls return journaled outputs without re-execution and only the in-flight call re-runs.

PROBLEM: A handler must pause until an external party (human, webhook, another service) resolves something, without holding a worker thread.
MECHANISM: Awakeable journal entries create an ID addressable from outside. crates/ingress-http/src/handler/awakeables.rs exposes HTTP POST resolve/reject on the awakeable ID; resolving completes the journal entry and wakes the handler. Combined with the Sleep entry, this covers timer-wake and external-wake uniformly. CompleteAwakeable is itself journaled, so resolution survives crashes.
INVARIANT: An awakeable is resolved at most once; the resolution is journaled before the waiter wakes. No worker resource is held while waiting.
FAILURE_MODEL: Lost resolution (crash between external resolve and journaling) = waiter sleeps until a timeout or manual intervention. Awakeable IDs are bearer tokens: anyone with the ID can resolve.
SECURITY_MODEL: Bearer-token by ID; no additional auth in the OSS path. This is the weak point: ID leakage = external control of execution flow.
SCALING_MODEL: Resolution routed to the owning partition.
CRX_ANALOG: This is the human-approval primitive CRX lacks. An approval gate = create awakeable (journaled), hand the ID to the approval surface (Nolan), suspend the attempt with zero worker held; approval resolves it. CRX must add authorization at resolve time (Restate's bearer-token model is insufficient for CRX's action-level auth gap).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Restate awakeables resolve with arbitrary bytes. CRX approvals must resolve with a typed, signed decision (approve/deny + rationale + identity of approver) recorded as evidence.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: awakeable table (id, attempt, created, resolved, timeout), resolve endpoint with auth, journal entry type. Reimplement, do not copy (BSL-1.1 + bearer-token model unsuitable).
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: unblocks human-in-the-loop without polling or held workers; the foundation of the approval gate.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Create an awakeable, kill all workers, resolve it externally, restart; assert the attempt wakes with the resolution and the resolution is journaled (resolving twice is rejected).

PROBLEM: Every unit of durable work needs a globally unique, routable, stable identity across crashes and retries.
MECHANISM: crates/types/src/identifiers.rs: InvocationId = partition_key (routing) + InvocationUuid(u128) (uniqueness). The ID encodes where the invocation lives and uniquely names it; AttachInvocation and GetInvocationOutput let other parties rendezvous on an invocation by ID.
INVARIANT: One invocation ID names exactly one logical execution across all retries and recoveries.
FAILURE_MODEL: UUID collision is negligible; partition-key mismatch misroutes.
SECURITY_MODEL: IDs are opaque; knowledge of an ID grants attach/output access (bearer-ish).
SCALING_MODEL: Partition key embedded in the ID enables routing without a lookup.
CRX_ANALOG: Directly fills CRX's proven gap: no durable per-attempt Run identity. CRX attempt IDs should be (mission ID, attempt sequence, UUIDv7) with the mission ID embedded for routing/lineage, exactly this shape.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Restate embeds a partition key for its sharded runtime. CRX embeds the mission ID for causation lineage. Same shape, different routing key.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: define the attempt-ID format and use it as the primary key of the attempt record and step journal.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: the identity foundation everything else (journal, heartbeats, signals, approval) keys off. Without it, none of the other mechanisms have a stable subject.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Generate 1M attempt IDs; assert uniqueness, correct embedded mission ID, and that attempt lookup by ID needs no secondary index.

PROBLEM: A function must sleep until a time, wait for a matching event, or wait for a named signal, then resume exactly where it left off, surviving executor restarts.
MECHANISM: pkg/execution/state/pause.go: the Pause struct is the unified suspend record: ID (V7 UUID), Identifier (run to resume), Outgoing/Incoming edge (where in the DAG), Expires (TTL, required), Event + Expression (resume when a matching event arrives), SignalID (named signal rendezvous), OnTimeout (traverse the timeout edge only if the event was NOT received), DataKey (where to store the resumed payload in run state). PauseMutater (SavePause/DeletePause/PausesByEvent) is the storage interface. A sleep is a pause with only Expires; a waitForEvent is a pause with Event+Expression; a signal wait is a pause with SignalID.
INVARIANT: One pause record fully describes how to resume. Expiry is mandatory, so no pause waits forever. The timeout branch is evaluated against the unconsumed pause, giving clean timeout-vs-event semantics.
FAILURE_MODEL: Executor death while paused is a non-event: the pause record is the state. Lost pause record = run stalls until manual intervention (no self-healing redrive observed in this code path). Clock skew affects Expires evaluation.
SECURITY_MODEL: Workspace-scoped; expression matching is server-side.
SCALING_MODEL: Pauses indexed by event name for O(matching) resume; Redis-backed in production.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX's sleep/wake and signal-wait should be one record type, not three mechanisms. A CRX Suspend record: {attempt ID, resume point, expires (mandatory), resume-on (event pattern | signal ID | nothing), on-timeout behavior, payload key}. This directly serves the CRX run-rotation and approval machinery.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Inngest pauses resume a function DAG edge. CRX suspends resume an agent attempt at a decision boundary, and the resume payload must be evidence-graded (CONFIRMED/STRONG/WEAK/UNKNOWN per CRX standards).
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: suspend-record table + matcher + timeout sweeper. Reimplement; SSPL-1.0 forbids embedding Inngest code in a hosted service context.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: unifies sleep, event-wait, and signal-wait into one auditable record; mandatory expiry kills the 'stalled forever' class of bugs.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Create a pause with Event+Expression and Expires; publish a non-matching event (assert no resume), then a matching event (assert resume with payload at DataKey); create another and let it expire (assert OnTimeout edge traversed, not the event edge).

PROBLEM: Function code must declare durable boundaries (steps) in a way the executor can persist, replay, and resume.
MECHANISM: pkg/execution/state/opcode.go: the executor interprets a small opcode set from the SDK: OpcodeStepRun, OpcodeSleep, OpcodeWaitForEvent, OpcodeInvoke, etc. Each opcode maps to a step type and has typed options (WaitForEventOpts, SleepDuration). The opcode stream IS the durable program: replay re-interprets opcodes against stored step state instead of re-running user code.
INVARIANT: User code never runs twice for the same step; the opcode log decides. Deterministic replay is structural, not a convention.
FAILURE_MODEL: Non-deterministic user code between steps (random IDs, wall-clock reads) breaks replay identity; Inngest mitigates with step IDs and memoization, not by solving determinism.
SECURITY_MODEL: Opcodes arrive from the SDK over the wire; the executor trusts the function to emit a consistent opcode stream.
SCALING_MODEL: Stateless interpretation; step state in the store.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX agent attempts are currently opaque blobs. An opcode-like step protocol for attempts (TOOL_CALL, SUBAGENT_SPAWN, FILE_WRITE, SLEEP, WAIT_SIGNAL, CHECKPOINT) would make attempts replayable and auditable. This is the structural fix for 'memory retrieval absent from execution path': retrieval becomes an opcode with a journaled result.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Inngest opcodes are SDK-emitted. CRX steps are agent-emitted and adversarial (the agent may lie about what it did); CRX must verify step claims against evidence (e.g. tool-call opcodes reconciled with actual MCP/tool receipts), not trust them.
INTEGRATION_COST: High: define the attempt step protocol, instrument the executor, journal results. This is the deepest integration in this file.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Very high: turns opaque attempts into replayable, verifiable step streams; prerequisite for real replay and for the MCP/tool-execution path gap.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Run an attempt emitting TOOL_CALL opcodes, kill mid-run, replay; assert completed tool calls return journaled outputs and the replayed step stream is byte-identical to the live one.

PROBLEM: Event producers retry; the same logical event must not create duplicate runs.
MECHANISM: pkg/event/id.go: SeededIDFromString parses an idempotency-key header of the form 'millis,base64(10-byte entropy)' and derives deterministic ULIDs: ULID = (millis, entropy + index). The same key with per-event index yields stable, unique IDs per event in a batch. Dedup is then a primary-key insert: same key = same ULID = conflict = duplicate suppressed.
INVARIANT: Idempotency key -> deterministic ULID. Retried submissions converge to the same IDs without a lookup.
FAILURE_MODEL: Key reuse across different logical events causes wrongful dedup (producer bug). Millis must be > 0; malformed keys are rejected, not defaulted.
SECURITY_MODEL: Producer-supplied; no verification of key ownership.
SCALING_MODEL: No coordination: deterministic derivation is local.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX mission starts and tool calls need producer-side idempotency keys with deterministic derivation. A subagent spawn request carries (request key); the attempt ID derives deterministically, so parent retries converge instead of duplicating.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Inngest derives ULIDs for events. CRX derives attempt IDs and step IDs from (mission ID, key). Same math, CRX keyspace.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: adopt the (millis, entropy+index) derivation for CRX request keys.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: cheap, removes a class of duplicate-spawn bugs.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Submit the same batch with the same idempotency key twice; assert identical ULIDs and exactly one run created.

PROBLEM: Individual steps fail transiently; the whole function should not.
MECHANISM: pkg/execution/executor/executor.go: per-step RetryCount() from the function definition, item.MaxAttempts set per queue item, and queue.ShouldRetry(err, attempt, maxRetries) gates re-enqueue. Retries are per-step: a failed step retries without re-running earlier completed steps (their outputs are in step state).
INVARIANT: Completed steps never re-run on a later step's retry. Retry budget is per-step, declared in code.
FAILURE_MODEL: Retry budget exhaustion fails the run; non-idempotent step side effects duplicate on retry (at-least-once steps).
SECURITY_MODEL: Retry counts are author-declared.
SCALING_MODEL: Re-enqueue through the normal queue path.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX attempt steps (tool calls) need per-step retry budgets distinct from attempt-level retry. A flaky MCP tool call retries the call, not the whole subagent attempt.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Inngest steps are deterministic functions. CRX steps are agent tool calls with costs; retry budgets must account for cost, not just count.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-Medium: retry budget on the step record; ShouldRetry predicate over CRX failure taxonomy.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: avoids whole-attempt retries for single flaky tool calls; big cost saver.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Fail a tool call twice then succeed with RetryCount=3; assert earlier steps did not re-execute and the attempt completes.

PROBLEM: A run must pause for an out-of-band decision (human approval, third-party webhook) with a deadline, resumable by a party that knows nothing about the run's internals.
MECHANISM: packages/trigger-sdk/src/v3/wait.ts: wait.createToken({idempotencyKey, timeout, tags}) mints a token with a completion URL; wait.forToken(token).unwrap() suspends the run until the token is completed (status/comment payload) or the timeout fires (WaitpointTimeoutError). Completion is by any party holding the token URL (e.g. passed as a webhook URL to Replicate). IdempotencyKey on creation makes token minting itself idempotent.
INVARIANT: One token, one completion. Timeout always resolves the wait (never hangs). The completer needs only the token, not run internals.
FAILURE_MODEL: Token URL leakage = anyone can complete the wait (bearer capability). Lost token = wait resolves by timeout only.
SECURITY_MODEL: Bearer URL. No approver identity is recorded by the primitive itself.
SCALING_MODEL: Token state server-side; completion is an API call.
CRX_ANALOG: The approval-gate UX pattern CRX needs: mint an approval token per gate, hand Nolan (or a webhook) a URL, suspend the attempt. CRX must strengthen the primitive: typed decision payload, approver identity, and evidence linkage (who approved, when, with what context shown).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Trigger waitpoints are bearer-URL capabilities. CRX approvals are evidence events: the resolution must record approver identity and the exact prompt shown, for replay and audit.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: token mint/resolve API with auth and typed payloads; Apache-2.0 SDK code can be referenced.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: the concrete UX shape of human approval (URL handoff + timeout + idempotent minting).
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Mint a token with idempotencyKey X twice; assert one token. Complete it; assert the waiter resumes with the payload. Let a second token expire; assert WaitpointTimeoutError, not a hang.

PROBLEM: A running task must be suspendable mid-execution (deploy, scale-down, waitpoint) and restorable on a different worker.
MECHANISM: packages/core/src/v3/schemas/checkpoints.ts: CheckpointServiceSuspendRequestBody {type: CheckpointType, runId, snapshotId, runnerId, projectRef, deploymentVersion, reason} and CheckpointServiceRestoreRequestBody (dequeue message with checkpoint: true). Suspend captures a snapshot ID; restore rehydrates the run from the snapshot on dequeue. The runner that suspended is named (runnerId) so orphaned snapshots are attributable.
INVARIANT: Suspend always names its snapshot; restore always loads by snapshot ID. A run is either running on exactly one runner or suspended with a named snapshot.
FAILURE_MODEL: Snapshot write failure during suspend = run state uncertain (the reason field exists for post-mortem). Restore of a corrupt snapshot fails the run.
SECURITY_MODEL: Runner-authenticated API.
SCALING_MODEL: Snapshots in object storage; restore on any runner.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX run rotation and worker migration need exactly this: suspend names (run ID, snapshot ID, worker ID, reason); restore is a dequeue with the snapshot. The 'reason' field is the audit hook CRX's evidence model wants.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Trigger snapshots are opaque VM/container state. CRX snapshots are (mission state, evidence pointers, conversation summary); the snapshot format is CRX-constitutional.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: snapshot/restore protocol on the run record; snapshot store.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: enables worker migration and clean run rotation without bespoke code per case.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Suspend a run mid-execution, terminate its worker, restore on a new worker; assert continuation from the snapshot with identical observable state.

PROBLEM: The orchestrator must know whether the worker holding a run is alive.
MECHANISM: packages/core/src/v3/heartbeats/: HeartbeatsManager with startHeartbeat(id)/stopHeartbeat()/lastHeartbeat. The SDK heartbeats while a run executes; the server treats heartbeat silence as worker death and requeues the run.
INVARIANT: A run is owned by a worker iff heartbeats are fresh. Silence transfers ownership back to the queue.
FAILURE_MODEL: Same partition-vs-death ambiguity as all heartbeats; heartbeat interval vs detection latency tradeoff.
SECURITY_MODEL: Worker-authenticated.
SCALING_MODEL: Per-run heartbeat state; server-side sweeper.
CRX_ANALOG: Same as TEMPORAL-ACTIVITY-HEARTBEAT-TIMEOUT but at run granularity. CRX can implement one heartbeat path (attempt-level) and treat run-level as derived.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Minimal; heartbeat semantics are generic infrastructure.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low (fold into the attempt-heartbeat mechanism).
EXPECTED_VALUE: Low as a separate mechanism; value captured under TEMPORAL-ACTIVITY-HEARTBEAT-TIMEOUT.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Stop heartbeats mid-run; assert the run is requeued within the detection window.

PROBLEM: Multiple scheduler replicas must coordinate queue, worker, and concurrency-slot assignment without split-brain.
MECHANISM: pkg/scheduling/v1/lease_manager.go: LeaseManager holds tenant-scoped leases (workerLeases, queueLeases, concurrencyLeases, batchLeases) backed by Postgres (v1.LeaseRepository). A scheduler instance only schedules what it holds a lease on; leases expire and are re-acquired, so a dead scheduler's queues are picked up by survivors. Multiplexes lease events to subscribers via notifier channels.
INVARIANT: At most one scheduler actively schedules a given queue/worker set at a time (lease-gated). Lease loss = stop scheduling, not corrupt scheduling.
FAILURE_MODEL: Lease expiry during a scheduling decision can cause duplicate assignment; the task layer must be idempotent to tolerate it. Clock skew shortens effective leases.
SECURITY_MODEL: Tenant-scoped; leases never cross tenants.
SCALING_MODEL: Postgres-backed; lease churn is the scaling bottleneck, bounded by tenant count.
CRX_ANALOG: If CRX ever runs multiple scheduler replicas (or parent agents), work assignment needs lease-gating: a parent only assigns attempts it holds a lease on. For single-scheduler CRX, the pattern still applies to worker slots: an attempt occupies a worker slot under a lease; slot lease expiry frees stuck attempts.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Hatchet leases gate scheduler replicas. CRX leases gate attempt-to-worker assignment and slot occupancy. Same primitive, different resource.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: lease table (resource, holder, expires); acquire/renew/release; scheduler honors leases. MIT code can be referenced.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: required before CRX scales past one scheduler; prevents duplicate assignment today in the worker-slot form.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill the scheduler holding queue leases; assert a survivor acquires them and no task is assigned twice (or duplicates are idempotently absorbed).

PROBLEM: Durable tasks need replayable records of what ran, what was waited on, and what was memoized.
MECHANISM: pkg/repository/durable_events.go + pkg/repository/sqlcv1/models.go: V1DurableEventLogKind = RUN | WAIT_FOR | MEMO. RUN records durable task executions (with TaskExternalId/NodeId/BranchId addressing into the DAG), WAIT_FOR records external-signal wait conditions (IngestWaitForOpts with label for humans), MEMO records memoization entries (MemoKey -> payload) so replayed deterministic computations return cached results. durable_events_dag_replay_test.go proves DAG replay from the log.
INVARIANT: Every durable action leaves a typed log record. Replay is a fold over the log; memoization makes deterministic re-execution free.
FAILURE_MODEL: Log write must be atomic with the action's commit; otherwise replay diverges. MEMO key collisions across different computations cause wrong-result replay (key must include the computation identity).
SECURITY_MODEL: Tenant-scoped.
SCALING_MODEL: Postgres; log partitioned by tenant/task.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX's ping_events is the RUN log. CRX lacks the WAIT_FOR record (signal waits as first-class log entries) and the MEMO record (memoized deterministic computations, e.g. cached research results, embeddings). Adding both as event types closes real gaps.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Hatchet's DAG is static. CRX's 'DAG' is agent-decided at runtime; the log records what the agent actually did, which is strictly more general.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-Medium: two new ping_events types (signal_wait, memo) with schemas; MIT code referenceable.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium-High: memoization alone saves repeated expensive computations across attempts.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Record a MEMO entry, replay the computation; assert the cached payload is returned without re-execution. Record WAIT_FOR, deliver the signal after a crash; assert the waiter resumes.

PROBLEM: Concurrent duplicate submissions with the same idempotency key must resolve to one execution.
MECHANISM: pkg/repository/idempotency.go: ClaimIdempotencyKeysOpt {ExpiresAt, Key, ClaimedByExternalId}; ClaimKey(tenant, key, expiresAt, claimedBy) returns (bool, error): test-and-set claim with TTL in Postgres. The winner proceeds; losers see the claim and attach to the winner's execution. Expired claims are evicted (EvictExpiredIdempotencyKeys).
INVARIANT: Key claim is atomic. Exactly one claimant wins; the claim names the winning execution so losers can rendezvous.
FAILURE_MODEL: Winner crashes before recording the execution ID: claim holds the key but points nowhere until TTL expiry. TTL too long = duplicate suppression window too long; too short = duplicate execution.
SECURITY_MODEL: Tenant-scoped keys.
SCALING_MODEL: Single-row atomic claim; Postgres serializes.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX spawn and tool-call dedup should use claim-with-TTL, not just deterministic IDs: the claim records WHICH attempt won, so a duplicate requester can attach to the live attempt instead of merely being rejected.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Generic infrastructure; no CRX-specific semantics except the keyspace.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: idempotency_claims table + claim/attach logic. MIT license permits direct port.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: strictly better than reject-duplicate; gives 'attach to in-flight' semantics.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Two concurrent spawns with the same key; assert one attempt, both callers attached to it. Kill the winner pre-commit; assert the key becomes claimable after TTL.

PROBLEM: Workers that die without deregistering must stop receiving work.
MECHANISM: pkg/repository/sqlcv1/workers.sql.go: workers carry lastHeartbeatAt; cleanupOldWorkers deletes workers with lastHeartbeatAt older than a threshold (tenant-scoped, batched). Scheduling only considers live workers; assigned-but-unacked tasks on dead workers return to the queue.
INVARIANT: Schedulable = heartbeat-fresh. The dead-worker set is recomputed by a sweeper, not by the workers themselves.
FAILURE_MODEL: Sweeper lag = dead workers receive assignments briefly; assignment must therefore be a lease the worker acks, not a point of no return.
SECURITY_MODEL: Internal.
SCALING_MODEL: Batched cleanup queries.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX worker registry (subagent executors) needs the same sweeper: heartbeat-fresh = assignable; stale = drained and its attempts re-driven through the recovery path.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Generic infrastructure.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: worker heartbeats table + periodic sweeper (fold into attempt-heartbeat work).
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: the machine-death half of liveness; complements attempt-level heartbeats.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill a worker without deregistering; assert it stops receiving assignments after the sweep and its in-flight attempts are re-driven.

PROBLEM: An agent graph's state must persist between invocations so execution can pause, resume, branch, and time-travel.
MECHANISM: libs/checkpoint/langgraph/checkpoint/base/__init__.py: Checkpoint TypedDict {v (format version), id (unique AND monotonically increasing), ts, channel_values (per-channel state snapshot), channel_versions (monotonic per-channel versions), versions_seen (per-node channel versions, used to compute which nodes run next), updated_channels}. BaseCheckpointSaver: thread_id is the primary key; put/get_tuple/put_writes; copy from source_thread_id to target_thread_id (fork/branch). Checkpoint id ordering gives total order without timestamps.
INVARIANT: State = fold of channel updates; versions_seen decides the runnable set deterministically. Monotonic checkpoint IDs make 'latest' unambiguous.
FAILURE_MODEL: Checkpoint write failure mid-put = torn state; savers must write atomically. Non-serializable channel values fail loudly at put time.
SECURITY_MODEL: None in the saver interface; left to the store.
SCALING_MODEL: Keyed by thread_id; each thread is independent.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX attempts need exactly this snapshot shape: per-channel (per-concern) values with monotonic versions, so a resumed attempt knows what each subagent saw. The versions_seen map is the mechanism that makes 'which step runs next' deterministic after resume. Copy-between-threads = CRX run forking/branching.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: LangGraph channels are programmer-defined. CRX channels are constitutional concerns (evidence, plan, findings); the channel set is CRX-owned.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: checkpoint schema on the attempt record; versions_seen computation at resume. MIT code referenceable.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: the state-shape that makes resume/branch/time-travel correct; directly serves run rotation and recovery.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Checkpoint mid-run, kill, resume from the checkpoint; assert the runnable set computed from versions_seen equals the pre-crash runnable set and no step re-runs.

PROBLEM: An agent must be able to stop mid-node, ask a human a typed question, and resume with the answer, without losing state.
MECHANISM: libs/langgraph/langgraph/types.py: interrupt(value, response_schema) raises inside a node; the interrupt is captured as an Interrupt {value (the question/payload), id (stable interrupt ID), response_schema (expected answer shape)}. Execution suspends with the checkpoint intact. Resume via Command(resume={interrupt_id: answer} | single value). Multiple interrupts are keyed by ID, so parallel approval gates resolve independently.
INVARIANT: Interrupts are values in the checkpoint, not control flow. Resume is a data command mapping interrupt IDs to answers; replaying the checkpoint reproduces the interrupt instead of re-asking.
FAILURE_MODEL: Answer failing response_schema validation is rejected at resume (typed gate). Lost interrupt ID = unresolvable gate (IDs are stable in the checkpoint, so this means checkpoint loss).
SECURITY_MODEL: None built-in; the answer is trusted. CRX must not inherit this: answers need provenance.
SCALING_MODEL: In-checkpoint; no extra infra.
CRX_ANALOG: The cleanest human-approval primitive in the survey: typed question (response_schema), stable ID, data-only resume. CRX approval gates should be interrupt records: {gate ID, prompt shown, schema, raised-by attempt, answered-by, answer, answered-at}. Resume = Command-like decision event with causation link.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: LangGraph trusts the answer. CRX must evidence-grade it: who answered, what they saw, schema validation, and the answer becomes an evidence event, not just control-flow data.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: interrupt as a first-class journal/checkpoint entry + typed resume command. MIT code referenceable.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Very high: the approval primitive with the best replay story (interrupts survive in checkpoints; resume is data).
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Raise two interrupts in one node, checkpoint, kill, resume with Command(resume={id1: a1}); assert id2 still pending, id1 resolved with schema-validated a1, and replay of the checkpoint reproduces both interrupts.

PROBLEM: Every run and task needs a shared, queryable lifecycle vocabulary, including a distinct state for infrastructure failure.
MECHANISM: src/prefect/client/schemas/objects.py: StateType = SCHEDULED, PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, CRASHED, PAUSED, CANCELLING; TERMINAL_STATES = {COMPLETED, CANCELLED, FAILED, CRASHED}. The load-bearing distinction: CRASHED (infrastructure died: process killed, machine lost, no result produced) vs FAILED (code ran and raised). Orchestration rules transition states server-side; clients propose, server disposes.
INVARIANT: State transitions are validated server-side; illegal transitions are rejected. CRASHED is terminal and never produced by user code, only by the infrastructure detecting death.
FAILURE_MODEL: Client/server state skew: the server is authoritative; clients reconcile on next contact. A run the server marks CRASHED cannot be 'un-crashed' by a late client heartbeat.
SECURITY_MODEL: State proposals are authenticated; orchestration rules are server-side and tamper-proof from workers.
SCALING_MODEL: State in Postgres; transitions are row updates.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX's typed failure semantics need exactly this split: ATTEMPT_CRASHED (worker died, outcome unknown, safe to retry) vs ATTEMPT_FAILED (agent concluded failure, retry only with new information). CRX currently risks conflating them. Server-side transition validation = CRX's fail-closed canonicalization extended to run state.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Prefect states are generic. CRX states must carry evidence links (what proved the crash) and causation (what the attempt was doing).
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: formalize the attempt state enum with CRASHED/FAILED split and server-validated transitions.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: the UNKNOWN_OUTCOME problem is half-solved by vocabulary alone: CRASHED means 'retry freely', FAILED means 'retry only with new info'.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill a worker mid-attempt and let one attempt raise a terminal error; assert the first is CRASHED and the second FAILED, and that an automated retry policy treats them differently.

PROBLEM: A flow must be able to suspend itself durably (for approval, for a timeout, for manual intervention) and be resubmitted later without holding any process.
MECHANISM: src/prefect/exceptions.py:310: Pause('Raised when a flow run is PAUSED and needs to exit for resubmission'). src/prefect/_flow_run_suspension.py: FlowRunSuspensionRequest carries the server-accepted Suspended state through the Pause control-flow path at the next orchestration boundary. The process EXITS; resumption is a fresh process resubmitted by the server. is_suspended_flow_run_state identifies the Suspended state by (is_paused() and name == 'Suspended').
INVARIANT: Suspend = persist state server-side + exit process. There is no suspended-but-resident process. Resume always starts clean.
FAILURE_MODEL: Crash between state-persist and exit = the run may be resubmitted twice; idempotent resubmission (same run ID) absorbs it. Exit without persist = run is CRASHED, not suspended.
SECURITY_MODEL: Suspension is self-requested; resume is server-driven.
SCALING_MODEL: Zero worker held during suspension; infinite suspend scale.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX subagents are processes/threads; a subagent that needs approval should Pause-and-exit, not block a slot. The attempt record holds the Suspended state; the approval resolution resubmits. This is cheaper than held-worker suspension and composes with the heartbeat mechanism (a suspended attempt needs no heartbeat).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Prefect resumes by resubmission to a worker pool. CRX resumes by spawning a fresh subagent with the checkpoint; the 'fresh process' property is what makes it safe.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-Medium: Suspended attempt state + resubmit-on-resolve path.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium-High: eliminates held-worker waits; the resource story that makes long approval gates affordable.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Suspend an attempt, assert its worker slot is freed and the process exited; resolve the gate; assert a fresh worker resumes from the persisted state with no duplicate work.

PROBLEM: After a failure, rerunning everything is wasteful; rerunning from the failure needs the event log to know what succeeded.
MECHANISM: python_modules/dagster/dagster/_core/execution/plan/resume_retry.py: ReexecutionStrategy = ALL_STEPS | FROM_FAILURE | FROM_ASSET_FAILURE. The run's event log (DagsterEventType: STEP_SUCCESS, STEP_FAILURE, RUN_SUCCESS...) records per-step outcomes durably; a re-execution plan is computed from the log: FROM_FAILURE replays only failed/skipped steps, reusing recorded outputs of successful ones.
INVARIANT: The event log is sufficient to compute the minimal re-execution plan. Successful steps are never re-executed in FROM_FAILURE mode.
FAILURE_MODEL: Steps with non-idempotent side effects that 'succeeded' in the log but whose effects were lost (downstream system rolled back) cause silent skips; FROM_FAILURE trusts the log absolutely.
SECURITY_MODEL: Run-scoped.
SCALING_MODEL: Log scan per re-execution; bounded by step count.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX attempt retry should default to FROM_FAILURE: compute the resume plan from the step journal, re-running only steps without recorded outputs. This is the reconciliation policy CRX needs, stated as an enum, not folklore.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Dagster steps are a static DAG; the plan is computed by graph traversal. CRX steps are a dynamic sequence; the plan is computed by journal prefix scan. Same strategy enum, different planner.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: reexecution-strategy field on retry; planner over the step journal.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: makes retries cheap and principled; prevents the 'retry reruns the expensive research step' waste.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Fail step 3 of 5 with recorded outputs for 1-2; retry with FROM_FAILURE; assert steps 1-2 not re-executed and step 3 reruns.

PROBLEM: Timers and scheduled starts can be lost (reminder dropped, scheduler failover gap); a workflow stuck in PENDING must be detected and re-driven without human intervention.
MECHANISM: pkg/actors/targets/workflow/common/pendingstart/pendingstart.go:64: Overdue(state, now) returns the pending event when now > DueTime + RedriveGrace(). pkg/runtime/wfengine/backends/actors/actors.go:185: redriveOverduePendingStart pokes the workflow actor with a one-shot status fetch whose handler re-asserts the overdue start reminder. Redrives are rate-limited (at most once per grace per instance, GoKeyed 'redrive||<id>') and detached (never block the status path).
INVARIANT: Every pending start has a due time; lateness past grace is observable from state alone; redrive is idempotent and rate-limited.
FAILURE_MODEL: Redrive of a genuinely-not-ready workflow is a no-op (handler re-checks). Grace too short = redrive storms during scheduler failover.
SECURITY_MODEL: Internal control plane.
SCALING_MODEL: Status reads trigger the check; no global sweeper needed (lazy reconciliation on read).
CRX_ANALOG: This is the reconciliation pattern CRX lacks: don't sweep the world on a timer; on every status read of a run/attempt, check (now > due + grace) and re-drive if overdue. Applies to: suspended attempts past resume time, heartbeats overdue, approval gates past SLA.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Dapr re-drives workflow starts. CRX re-drives attempt state transitions. The lazy-on-read reconciliation is the portable insight.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: an Overdue(state, now) predicate per suspend/lease record + re-drive on status read, rate-limited.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: self-healing for lost timers without a global sweeper; bounds stall duration by read frequency.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Lose a scheduled resume (delete the timer), read the attempt status; assert the re-drive fires, the resume is re-asserted, and repeated reads within the grace do not duplicate the re-drive.

PROBLEM: Workflow orchestration state must survive actor deactivation and sidecar restarts.
MECHANISM: The workflow backend persists WorkflowRuntimeState {History, CustomStatus, ...} in the workflow actor's state store (pkg/runtime/wfengine/backends/actors/actors.go:570: runtimestate.NewWorkflowRuntimeState(id, customStatus, history)). The durable-task history lives in actor state; reminders drive scheduling; the actor model gives single-threaded execution per workflow (no concurrent decision races).
INVARIANT: One actor = one workflow = one decision thread. History in actor state is the execution record.
FAILURE_MODEL: Actor state store loss = workflow loss (mitigated by replicated state stores). Reminder loss is handled by the redrive mechanism above.
SECURITY_MODEL: Actor invocation is app-authenticated.
SCALING_MODEL: Actors distributed by consistent hashing; placement service tracks.
CRX_ANALOG: The single-decider-per-run property is what CRX's parent agent needs: exactly one decision-maker per mission at a time, with its state durable. CRX should enforce single-decider as an invariant (lease), not a convention.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Dapr actors are the unit. CRX's unit is the mission; the decider lease is the portable piece.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: decider lease per mission (ties to HATCHET-LEASE-MANAGER).
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: prevents split-brain parent decisions, a real risk as CRX parallelizes.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Start two parent deciders for one mission; assert exactly one holds the lease and the other's decisions are rejected.

PROBLEM: After a crash, pending workflows must be recovered exactly once even if multiple executors attempt recovery concurrently.
MECHANISM: dbos/_recovery.py: _recover_workflow re-enqueues the workflow; 'Recovery re-enqueues rather than executing directly, so that every recovered workflow starts through the queue's atomic ENQUEUED->PENDING dequeue. That handoff admits exactly one runner, which makes duplicate recovery requests idempotent.' startup_recovery_thread runs recovery for local pending workflows on boot in a background thread.
INVARIANT: Recovery = enqueue, never direct execute. The atomic dequeue is the single serialization point; all duplicate recovery attempts converge through it.
FAILURE_MODEL: Recovery thread death = no recovery (supervisor must watch the thread). Queue loss = recovery target lost.
SECURITY_MODEL: Executor IDs scope which workflows an executor may recover.
SCALING_MODEL: Recovery is O(pending) at startup; steady-state recovery via the queue.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX's process/machine-death recovery should be: on startup (or on detecting a dead worker), move CRASHED attempts to a recovery queue; workers claim via atomic dequeue. Never 'resume in place' from the recovery path; always go through the claim. This makes recovery idempotent under concurrent detectors.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: DBOS recovers workflows. CRX recovers attempts. The enqueue-not-execute invariant is the portable core.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-Medium: recovery queue + atomic claim; startup scan for CRASHED attempts. MIT code referenceable.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: the crash-recovery path with no duplicate-execution hazard; composes with heartbeats (detector) and FROM_FAILURE (planner).
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Crash with 10 pending attempts; start two recovery detectors concurrently; assert each attempt is claimed exactly once and all 10 resume.

PROBLEM: UNKNOWN_OUTCOME: a step may have executed its side effect but crashed before reporting; on recovery, re-executing could duplicate the effect.
MECHANISM: dbos/_dbos.py + _sys_db.py: every step is recorded in the system DB as it completes ('the update is recorded as a step so it runs exactly once even if the workflow is recovered'). Recovery replays from the recorded step prefix: recorded steps return stored outputs; only unrecorded steps execute. Child workflow spawning is transactional: 'Insert a child's status row and record it as the parent's step in one transaction, so a crash leaves both or neither' (_sys_db.py:5201).
INVARIANT: Recorded = done, never re-executed. The record and the side effect commit atomically where possible (single DB transaction for DB-backed steps).
FAILURE_MODEL: Non-transactional side effects (external API calls) remain at-least-once; the recording bounds the re-execution to the unrecorded suffix, it does not make external calls idempotent. Crash between side effect and record = duplicate on recovery (the residual UNKNOWN_OUTCOME window).
SECURITY_MODEL: System DB is trusted; step records are authoritative.
SCALING_MODEL: One row per step in Postgres.
CRX_ANALOG: This is CRX's UNKNOWN_OUTCOME answer: the step journal with atomic (record step output + commit effects) where effects are CRX-internal, and explicit at-least-once labeling where effects are external (API calls, emails). Subagent spawn recorded atomically with the parent's step (mirrors the child-status-row transaction).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: DBOS steps are Python functions; many are DB-transactional. CRX steps are tool calls; most are NOT transactional, so CRX must label each step (transactional/at-least-once) and the retry planner must respect the label.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: step journal with per-step effect-class labels; atomic spawn recording. MIT code referenceable.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Very high: the precise, honest treatment of UNKNOWN_OUTCOME: shrink the window with atomic recording, label what remains, never pretend at-least-once is exactly-once.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Crash between an external API call and its step record; assert recovery re-executes the call AND the journal shows the step as at-least-once (not silently exactly-once). Crash between a DB-backed step's commit and record; assert atomicity holds (both or neither).

PROBLEM: Agents calling workflow tools need bounded, revokable authority scoped to their role and work unit; a stolen or stale credential must fail closed without manual revocation.
MECHANISM: Tool leases (src/registry-tool-leases.js): SHA-256-hashed bearer tokens scoped to (project, session, lane) with a role (orchestrator/executor/auditor/dashboard) and an explicit allowedTools subset; validateToolLease checks hash, revocation, expiry, role match, tool grant, and scope match on every call. Sliding renewal (etcd/Consul pattern): a lease used in the second half of its window is pushed to a full window again, max once per half-window, never reviving revoked/expired leases. Refresh credentials (OAuth2 pattern): long-lived (90d idle lapse) credentials that can do exactly one thing — exchange for a lease — and cannot call tools; revoking a credential revokes every lease it issued (credential tree). createToolLease's replaceActiveForActor revokes same-actor/same-scope active leases to prevent duplicate live agents. Lease cap 500 with active-first eviction so volume never 401s a live agent.
INVARIANT: Every agent tool call carries a live, unexpired, unrevoked lease whose role grants the tool and whose scope contains the target work; one live credential per actor+scope.
FAILURE_MODEL: State file holds all lease hashes in plaintext JSON (local disk trust); process death leaves leases valid until expiry (bounded by TTL); clock skew could extend/shorten windows; single local daemon is the only issuer.
SECURITY_MODEL: Token hashes never log plaintext (12-char hash prefix only); tokens returned once at mint; secret redaction on event enqueue; refresh credential != tool lease (validateToolLease rejects credentials); admin-gated bootstrap mint.
SCALING_MODEL: Single-node; 500-lease cap with active-first eviction; leases are small records in state.json; renewals bounded to once per half-window.
CRX_ANALOG: No MCP/tool-execution path exists (audit gap). Ingress-only authorization. CRX has worker runtime but no action-level capability tokens.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca implements ACTION->AUTHORIZATION->EXECUTION->RECEIPT at the tool-call layer with capability leases; CRX has authorization only at mission ingress. The refresh-credential exchange (lapsed lease heals on next exchange) matches CRX's 'bounded retries with evidence' doctrine.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: requires tool-execution path to exist first; lease issuer must be a canonical authority (identity+canonicalization), stored in PG not a second store.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Very high: the exact mechanism class CRX lacks (action-level authorization with receipts, gap #1/#2).
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Steal a lease token, expire it, revoke it, swap roles — each must 401/403. Kill the worker mid-lease; the next exchange must self-heal without human action.

PROBLEM: Agents call workflow tools out of order (accept before review, submit before running) or on stale lane state, corrupting lifecycle integrity.
MECHANISM: Workflow state gates (src/registry-tool-leases.js LANE_TOOL_STATE_GATES, enforced by assertAgentToolAllowed): each lifecycle tool is legal only in specific lane states (e.g. lane.submit only in [starting,running]; audit.accept only in [ready_for_audit,auditing,done]). A refused call returns 409 with a computed nextAction envelope pointing at the corrective tool, so the agent can self-correct from the error alone. Flexible ops (stop/retry/controls/evidence) deliberately stay ungated.
INVARIANT: A lifecycle tool call on a lane in a non-listed state is refused, never silently applied; every refusal names the remedy.
FAILURE_MODEL: Gates read lane.state from memory; if state.json was hand-edited, gates follow the lie (state is trusted post-restore). New states must be added to the gate map or tools become unreachable.
SECURITY_MODEL: Enforced server-side; the client cannot grant itself a tool the server did not lease, and cannot bypass the gate map.
SCALING_MODEL: O(1) per call; gate map is static data.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has typed failure semantics as doctrine but transitions scattered in runtime code; no per-tool legality map against run state.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca turns lifecycle legality into data (tool->allowed-states) with machine-actionable refusals; CRX has the doctrine, not the table. Complements orca-cli/orca O-2 (pure transition table).
INTEGRATION_COST: Very low: a static map + check in the tool-call path once tool execution exists.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: cheap, makes illegal transitions unrepresentable at the agent-tool layer, and gives agents a self-serve recovery path from every refusal.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Attempt audit.accept on a running lane and lane.submit on a queued lane; both must 409 with a nextAction envelope naming a legal tool.

PROBLEM: A spawned agent does not know what to do next: it must poll multiple endpoints and hold the whole workflow model in its prompt, burning context and mis-firing tools.
MECHANISM: Next-action envelope (src/agent-tools/next-action.js): every orchestrator.status (and every refusal) returns a computed envelope: loopState (lane state mapped to a named loop phase), nextRequiredTool (deterministic state machine: no project->register, no session->register, no lane->executor.spawn, queued->observe, running->lane.submit for executors, done->audit.queue_one etc.), nextToolPermitted (whether this role may call it), allowedTools, evidenceRequired/auditRequired/auditSatisfied flags, flow (template, auditTier, fixRouting, maxAuditLoops, loopsRemaining, escalated), capacity (approvedCapacity, activeAgents, idleSlots, spawnPolicy). chooseSessionLane ranks lanes by a priority table (audit.queue_one=30, lane.retry=40, executor.spawn=45, lane.get=50, lane.submit=80, orchestrator.status=90) then recency — the server picks the lane needing attention, not the agent.
INVARIANT: The server always answers 'what should I do next' deterministically from durable state; the agent never needs the workflow model to proceed.
FAILURE_MODEL: If the envelope lies (stale in-memory state), the agent follows it into a 409, which carries a corrected envelope — self-healing. Priority table is static; pathological starvation of low-priority lanes is possible in principle (recency tiebreak mitigates).
SECURITY_MODEL: nextToolPermitted reflects role+lease; the real call still enforces server-side.
SCALING_MODEL: O(lanes) per envelope; the 'lean' variant skips the capability matrix for polled endpoints.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX coordinator context carries this conversationally; nothing machine-readable tells a worker what to do next. Directly addresses campaign §18 (coordinator should do little intelligent work; agents own investigation).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca pushes the scheduling decision INTO the state query (chooseSessionLane+priority), so the agent's only job is to execute the named tool. CRX currently pushes this intelligence into the coordinator's context.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: needs durable task/lane state + a state machine; the envelope shape can be a projection over the PG event journal.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Very high: this is the mechanism that makes workers disposable and the coordinator boring — the envelope survives worker death; any fresh agent can continue from it.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill a worker mid-mission; a brand-new agent with only the envelope endpoint must resume correct sequencing with no coordinator briefing.

PROBLEM: Wakeups (lane finished, audit needed) get lost, duplicated, or delivered to the wrong consumer; a repeat of a still-pending condition should not spam, but a genuinely new occurrence after ack must wake again.
MECHANISM: Durable agent-event queue (src/registry-agent-queue.js): seq-numbered events persisted in state; dedupeKey collapses repeats of a STILL-PENDING condition into occurrences+updatedAt, but an occurrence after a consumer acked is enqueued as a fresh event (fixed bug: acked events used to absorb later occurrences). Drain CONSUMES: event.drain acks what it returns (per-consumer acks keyed role:actor, capped at 64 with keep-key retention). Role-based visibility (orchestrator sees targetRole orchestrator|any; dashboard sees all). Secret redaction on enqueue (key pattern + value pattern). afterSeq/limit/type filters; MAX_AGENT_QUEUE=1000.
INVARIANT: An unacked condition wakes a consumer exactly once per occurrence-batch; a new occurrence after ack is a new wakeup; drain never returns the same backlog twice to the same consumer.
FAILURE_MODEL: Queue lives in state.json (debounced persist); a crash before flush loses the enqueue — the wakeup is lost unless re-enqueued. afterSeq pagination can skip if consumer crashes between pages.
SECURITY_MODEL: Secrets redacted at enqueue; role-gated visibility; acks per consumer so one consumer cannot consume another's wakeup.
SCALING_MODEL: 1000-event cap; acks normalized and capped at 64 per event.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has no wakeup queue; subagent results are delivered by the runtime into parent context. Nothing durable survives worker death for re-delivery.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca's queue is pull-based durability for agent wakeups with ack semantics; CRX's delivery is push-into-conversation. The dedupe-key-collapse-but-new-after-ack rule is a subtle, correct at-least-once-with-dedupe semantic.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: implement as event-journal-backed outbox with per-consumer ack cursors rather than a separate queue store.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: wakeup durability is required for the interruption experiments (§22) and for missions surviving worker death.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Enqueue audit-required for a lane 3x pre-ack (must collapse to 1 with occurrences=3); ack; enqueue again (must create a NEW event); drain twice (second drain must return empty).

PROBLEM: After a hard daemon restart (SIGKILL), a lane's detached child process group survives with no supervisor — running, burning tokens, holding the worktree — while the persisted lane state says 'running'.
MECHANISM: Interrupted-lane recovery (src/registry-lifecycle.js recoverInterruptedLanes + _reapOrphanedLaneProcess): on boot, for every lane in a state that can hide a live child (not just starting/running — also ready_for_audit/fix_requested/accepted/blocked, since submit sets ready_for_audit without waiting for exit), verify the persisted pid STILL looks like an executor: ps -p <pid> and match the command against a binary pattern derived from the executor table (not hardcoded). PID-REUSE HAZARD handled: a reused pid by an unrelated process is never killed; generic-cli (node) orphans are deliberately left alone rather than risk killing the daemon itself. Reaped->SIGKILL the negative pgid (whole detached group). Then: lanes in starting/running are marked failed ('Controller restarted while lane was active'); lanes that already submitted keep their state (handoff stays auditable) with a log line. Missing ids/paths are repaired with safe defaults.
INVARIANT: No orphaned executor survives a hard restart unverified; a pid is never killed on identity-by-number alone.
FAILURE_MODEL: If ps is unavailable, nothing is reaped (fail-closed toward leaving orphans). Executor binaries renamed after spawn evade the pattern. A lane marked failed may have actually completed its side effects — UNKNOWN_OUTCOME is not reconciled, just recorded.
SECURITY_MODEL: Only the daemon's own executor binaries are killable; negative-pgid kill is scoped to the detached group.
SCALING_MODEL: O(lanes) ps calls at boot, 2s timeout each.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has typed worker-death failure (WORKER_DEATH) but no boot-time orphan reaping or pid-verification; the §22 interruption experiments will need exactly this.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca treats 'restart' as a recovery event with a typed protocol (verify identity -> reap -> mark failed or preserve handoff). CRX names the failure type but has no reaping mechanism.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: boot-time recovery routine + executor binary registry.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: prerequisite for the coordinator-death experiment; the pid-reuse guard is a reusable invariant for any supervisor.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Start a lane, SIGKILL the daemon, spawn an unrelated process reusing the pid (or simulate), restart: the unrelated process must survive and the lane must be marked failed.

PROBLEM: Frequent state writes (every log line, every event) with naive temp+rename can land OUT of issue order under I/O contention, letting a staler snapshot win the rename race and silently drop fresh state.
MECHANISM: Serialized atomic persistence (src/registry-persistence.js + src/state-store/io.js + recovery.js): persistState() debounces 250ms and bumps an SSE revision counter; _flushPersistTimer snapshots state at flush-ISSUE time and chains the write on _writeChain so the last-issued (freshest) snapshot is the last to hit disk (temp+rename, atomic). readJsonFileWithRecovery: primary->backup->fallback with corrupt-file quarantine (quarantined copy kept, never deleted). Versioned migrations (v1->v3, v2->v3, v3->v4) with byte-preserving backups; a failed migration BLOCKS all further writes (_persistBlocked) rather than overwriting the original. Recovery/migration outcomes are recorded as audit events (registry_state_recovered/registry_state_migrated). Lane journals flush before the snapshot so the snapshot never drops streams the journal failed to write (failed-journal lanes keep streams inline instead).
INVARIANT: The last-issued snapshot is the last to reach disk; a failed migration never overwrites the original; no recovery path silently deletes user state.
FAILURE_MODEL: Single-file state.json: corruption of BOTH primary and backup falls back to empty state (data loss, but announced). Debounce window (250ms) can lose the last writes before a crash.
SECURITY_MODEL: Journal dirs and state files created 0700/0600; corrupt files quarantined, not deleted.
SCALING_MODEL: State file was 525MB before v4 journals (documented in docs/audits/2026-09-10-state-bloat-diagnosis.md); v4 moved streams to per-lane JSONL. Single-node.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has PG journal (stronger durability) but the snapshot-write-ordering hazard and the migration-backup discipline are relevant to any CRX local state (worktree metadata, run ledgers).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca's durability is file-local with explicit ordering and recovery semantics; CRX's PG journal is the canonical authority. The harvest is the discipline (write-chain ordering, migration backups, quarantine-not-delete, recovery-as-audit-events), not the store.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: apply to CRX local persistence helpers.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium-high: directly applicable to CRX local-state files and to any SQLite/JSONL projections; the 'recovery emits audit events' pattern fits CRX's evidence model.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Crash mid-flush under I/O contention; the recovered state must be the freshest complete snapshot, and both the corrupt original and the backup must be present on disk.

PROBLEM: Self-approval and rubber-stamping: an executor's work is accepted with an empty verdict, or visual work is signed off sight-unseen, or audit->fix loops forever.
MECHANISM: Audit gate (src/registry-audit.js): acceptLaneAudit REFUSES accept unless at least one finding or reviewed file is recorded (current call OR a prior audit.findings.record on the lane) — 409 with a nextAction pointing at audit.findings.record; objects are read for text fields so '[object Object]' cannot satisfy the gate. targetUrl lanes (UI/browser) additionally require captured evidence (screenshot/artifact file in the lane's artifact dir) before accept. Audit loop budget: requestLaneFix counts loops; at maxAuditLoops (default 2, configurable 0-10) the lane ESCALATES to the user instead of looping. Fix routing per flow config: same-agent (lane.retry) or new-agent (executor.spawn). Accept on a still-running lane is refused. Audit queue dedupe: at most ONE pending audit follow-up per lane across both queue event types. Stuck-audit reconciliation (dispatchPendingAudits): lanes in 'auditing' with no live auditor/orchestrator get bounded re-dispatch (MAX_AUDIT_DISPATCHES=2) then escalation — unattended runs cannot hang. Accept triggers guarded worktree reclaim.
INVARIANT: No lane reaches 'accepted' without a recorded human/agent review artifact; no audit loop runs unbounded; no lane hangs in 'auditing' forever.
FAILURE_MODEL: The gate checks recorded text, not review quality — a vacuous finding ('looks good') passes the integrity gate. Auditor and executor are both agents; collusion is not modeled.
SECURITY_MODEL: Accept blocked while a process is live; policy evaluation can require approval for auditLane; audit events are append-only evidence.
SCALING_MODEL: Per-lane audit records capped at 50; findings 100, reviewedFiles 200 per record.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has reviewer-agent and merge-gate concepts in the factory lane but no formal accept-integrity gate, no loop budget, no stuck-verdict reconciliation.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca's gate is evidence-of-review (findings recorded) + budget + escalation; CRX's review vocabulary (from orca-cli O-5) lacks the enforcement. The 'objects cannot rubber-stamp' coercion (auditEntryText) is a real anti-manufactured-success control.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-medium: accept-gate rules + loop counter + escalation state on the review path.
